newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Nov CPI advances by 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Nov CPI advances by 0.3 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported that November consumer prices rose by 0.3 percent after an identical 0.3 percent rise in the prior month. Experts had expected consumer prices to advance by 0.3 percent in November.

ANTHONY KARYDAKIS, SENIOR FINANCIAL ECONOMIST, FIRST CHICAGO CAPITAL MARKETS: "There's not much of a story in CPI. It was very uneventful, with nothing extraordinary. All of the components seem to have behaved consistent with the trend."

"The overall impression the report leaves us with is inflation remains as well-behaved as we all thought it was. The year-over-year increases of 3.3 percent overall and 2.6 on the core mean that things are proceeding very normally. It was an average report, with nothing particularly alarming."
KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS: "The CPI numbers were in line with expectations. No surprises there.
"What we're continuing to find out is moderate growth, little or steady inflation continues. These are the ingredients that have helped fuel the bond-market rally up to now.

"I think we've seen the best in terms of inflation on the retail front. We probably will see some escalation as 1997 gets underway. Nothing of dramatic proportions, but I think the improvement is over with for now."

MARILYN SCHAJA, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST AT DONALDSON, LUFKIN AND JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: "I think that CPI number indicate that inflation is well contained -- similar to the details of the PPI report that came out yesterday -- with the overall being up 0.3 (percent) but the core, less food and energy, being up only 0.2 (percent).

"I don't see any extraneous factors that should be reversed the following month. If anything it looks the other way, like again the increase in apparel costs for the third month in a row. So this is a very good number."

SAMUEL KAHAN, PRESIDENT, A.S.K. FINANCIAL RESEARCH: "The CPI came in as expected both for the overall index as well as key components such as apparel, medical care, education and housing. The only surprise was a sharper than expected decline in new car prices which may be a seasonal phenomenon related to the introduction of new models rather than an actual price change. Inflation continues to remain low.
"After reviewing these nubmers, the Federal Reserve would see no reason to change policy."
DAVID ORR, CHIEF CAPITAL MARKETS ECONOMIST, FIRST UNION CORP: "There is nothing in either retail sales or CPI that would cause a Federal Reserve policy change.

"CPI looks like more of the same. The 0.2 percent core rate is what the Federal Reserve is watching because that figure is more reflective of the underlying fundamentals of the economy. This month's level is very comfortable for the Fed."
